item.research_question: Whether the deformation of pure molybdenum, a refractory metal with no known polymorphs, can ever be coupled with a structural transformation that leads to the emergence of new metastable crystalline lattices under high-stress conditions.
item.processing_route: In situ tensile testing inside a transmission electron microscope (TEM) at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder; loading controlled by intermittent displacement with a time resolution of 0.1 s; crack tip configuration {010}<001>.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature; local shear stress ~8 GPa; local tensile stresses ~20.7±2.6 GPa along [100] and ~5.6±2.3 GPa along [010]; strain rate in MD simulations 10^7 s^-1 at 300 K.
key_findings: A structural transformation from <001>-oriented body-centred cubic (bcc1) to <110>-oriented face-centred cubic (fcc) was observed at crack tips.
The fcc domains subsequently reverted to <111>-oriented body-centred cubic domains (bcc2), equivalent to a lattice rotation of 54.7°.
Approximately 15.4% tensile strain was accommodated through the bcc1→fcc→bcc2 sequence.
The fcc structure was identified as a well-defined metastable state with a lattice parameter a=0.409 nm.
The orientation relationship between bcc1 and fcc follows the Nishiyama–Wassermann (N–W) relationship: (110)bcc1//(111)fcc and [001]bcc1//[10-1]fcc.
The orientation relationship between fcc and bcc2 follows the Kurdjumov–Sachs (K–S) relationship: (1-11)fcc//(011)bcc2 and [10-1]fcc//[1-11]bcc2.
Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed the atomic shear mechanism along <110> for bcc1→fcc and along {111}fcc for fcc→bcc2.
Twinning was suppressed in the {010}<001> crack configuration, whereas twinning was activated in {001}<110> configurations.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that when the easy deformation path (dislocation slip and twinning) is suppressed or bypassed, extremely high shear stresses (>7 GPa) thermodynamically drive the energetically uphill bcc-to-fcc transition to release local stress concentration. The fcc phase acts as a metastable intermediate state bridging two bcc orientations via N–W and K–S crystallographic relationships, allowing for massive shear deformation and lattice rotation without conventional twinning.
item.limitations: The intermediate fcc phase is difficult to detect in bulk samples or uniaxial tests because the transformation progresses rapidly to the final bcc state without confinement; the phase is only observable in localized, well-confined deformation areas like crack tips in nanometer-scaled samples.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that phase transformations coupled with large shear deformation or catastrophic yielding may occur in high-stress deformation conditions for other elemental metals without polymorphs, implying the mechanism is important for nanomaterials deformed under high-stress conditions.
quotes: Plastic deformation via structural transitions has never been reported for pure molybdenum, while transformation coupled with plasticity is well known for many alloys and ceramics.

The face-centred cubic structure appears to be a well-defined metastable state, as evidenced by scanning transmission electron microscopy and nanodiffraction, the Nishiyama–Wassermann and Kurdjumov–Sachs relationships between the face-centred cubic and body-centred cubic structures and molecular dynamics simulations.
An extremely high applied shear stress >7 GPa in this work) is necessary to thermodynamically drive the low-energy-state bcc Mo into the high-energy-state fcc Mo.
